passage: On the dusty patch behind the panchayat office, Lokesh and three other boys were playing marbles. Ujjwal, the oldest, nudged his marble closer to the hole with his toe when he thought nobody saw. Lokesh saw. His face went hot. "You moved it! I saw your foot!" "I didn't." "You did! That's cheating!" Lokesh's voice cracked, and he stamped so hard the dust flew up. The smaller boys looked from one to the other. Lokesh scooped up his own marbles. "I'm not playing if we don't play fair." He stood there, breathing fast, until Ujjwal kicked the marble back.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal move his marble?
qa.a: He nudged it closer to the hole with his toe.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's cracking voice and stamping suggest?
qa.a: He felt a burst of anger at the unfairness, strong enough to shake his voice.

qa.q: Which part of Lokesh's reaction helped, and what could be calmer?
qa.a: Refusing to play unless it was fair worked; saying it in a steadier voice could keep the fight from growing.

qa.q: How might the smaller boys have seen the argument?
qa.a: They may have been nervous to take sides against the oldest boy, but relieved when someone stood up for fair play.

grounding: It shows a boy's hot reaction to seeing a peer cheat in a game.

passage: In the lunch queue at their school in Manchester, two older boys slid in front of Sofia, laughing. The dinner lady didn't see. Kwame, eleven, felt heat climb up his neck. "Oi, that's not fair, she's been waiting!" he said, louder than he meant. The boys shrugged. "So?" Kwame's fists curled. "So go to the back like everyone else." Sofia tugged his sleeve. "Leave it." But Kwame stepped out of line and told the dinner lady, pointing. When the boys were sent to the back, his hands were still shaking.

qa.q: Where did the older boys push in?
qa.a: In front of Sofia in the lunch queue.

qa.q: Why were Kwame's hands still shaking after the boys were sent back?
qa.a: His anger at the unfairness was still running through him even after things were put right.

qa.q: What went well, and what could Kwame watch out for?
qa.a: Telling the dinner lady fixed it without a fight; he could notice his curled fists so the heat doesn't turn into shoving.

qa.q: Why might Sofia have said "Leave it"?
qa.a: She may have wanted to avoid trouble or attention, even though the unfairness was done to her.

grounding: It shows a boy's heated reaction to queue-jumping and rule-breaking against a classmate.

passage: At the swimming club's Sunday race, Nitin dived a moment before the whistle. People in the stands saw it, but the official didn't call him back, and he won by a hand. Elizabeth, eleven, came second. She climbed out and slapped the water off her arms. "He went early! Everyone saw!" Her cheeks were red, and she wouldn't step onto the podium. "It's not about losing. Rules are rules." The coach put a towel round her. "I'll speak to the official." Elizabeth sat on the bench, jaw tight, still watching Nitin grin with his medal.

qa.q: Where did Elizabeth finish in the race?
qa.a: She came second.

qa.q: What does Elizabeth refusing the podium show?
qa.a: She was burning with anger at the early start and didn't want to accept a result she saw as unfair.

qa.q: What would you advise Elizabeth to do next?
qa.a: Let the coach raise it with the official and perhaps take her podium place, since the complaint can go through the proper channel.

qa.q: How might Nitin see things differently?
qa.a: He may not realise he went early, or may not want to admit it, and sees only his win.

grounding: It shows a girl's heated sense of injustice when a rival breaks the start rule and wins.

passage: I'm Elizabeth, Rajni's neighbour. Yesterday the kids were playing ludo on our steps. One boy moved his token two extra squares when he thought no one saw. Rajni did see. She jumped up, face red. 'You cheated! That's not fair! You can't just do that!' She swept the tokens off the board. The boy said, 'It was a mistake.' Rajni stood there with her fists clenched, breathing hard. I thought she might cry. I don't know if it was just the game, but she was very angry.

qa.q: How many extra squares did the boy move his token?
qa.a: He moved it two extra squares.

qa.q: What does Rajni sweeping the tokens off the board suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a strong, hot anger at the unfairness of the cheating.

qa.q: What could Rajni do instead next time she spots cheating?
qa.a: She could say calmly what she saw and ask to replay the move, so the game stays fair without ending it.

qa.q: How might the boy who cheated feel after Rajni's outburst?
qa.a: He might feel embarrassed and defensive, which is why he claimed it was a mistake.

grounding: Illustrates a child reacting with emotional heat to cheating in a game, seen by a neighbour.

passage:
Monday: in the class quiz, Chinmay saw Eshaan's team peeking at a textbook under the desk. They won. Chinmay slammed his hand on the bench. 'They cheated!' The teacher said to sit down.
Tuesday: Chinmay was still fuming at lunch. 'It's not fair. We studied!'
Friday: he found the teacher alone. 'Sir, I saw them looking in the book.' The teacher listened and said he would watch more carefully next time. Chinmay walked away, jaw still tight, but his shoulders dropped a little.

qa.q: What did Chinmay see Eshaan's team doing?
qa.a: He saw them peeking at a textbook under the desk.

qa.q: Why was Chinmay still fuming on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt angry and frustrated that the win was unfair, because his team had studied honestly.

qa.q: What was wise about how Chinmay handled it on Friday?
qa.a: He waited until he was calmer and spoke to the teacher privately, which got him listened to.

qa.q: How might Eshaan's team feel if they knew Chinmay had told the teacher?
qa.a: They might feel embarrassed or worried about being caught next time.

grounding: Shows a child's heated reaction to cheating in a quiz and how it plays out over several days.

passage: "Saurabh, you're angry about the umpire? Let me tell you. When I, your Madhav Dadu, was ten, we played marbles every evening under the peepal tree. There was a boy who moved his marble closer when he thought no one saw. I saw. My face went hot, and I shouted, 'Cheat!' so loudly that the whole street stopped. He said I was lying. I didn't back down. I drew the line again in the dust and said, 'We start from here, properly.' The other boys agreed, and he played fair after that."

qa.q: Where did they play marbles?
qa.a: Under the peepal tree.

qa.q: What was young Madhav feeling when his face went hot?
qa.a: He was angry and indignant at seeing the boy cheat.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the game fair again?
qa.a: Madhav redrawing the line and getting the others to agree to restart properly.

qa.q: How might the boy who cheated have felt when everyone agreed to restart?
qa.a: Probably embarrassed and exposed, which pushed him to play fair.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling his childhood anger at a peer's cheating and how he insisted on fairness.

passage: The inter-house race went on despite the rain. Naveen, eleven, was running second when he saw a boy ahead cut across the muddy corner behind the tree, where the teachers couldn't see. The boy finished first. Naveen crossed second, soaked and furious. "He cheated!" he told his friend Shankar, his fists clenched. "Everyone saw!" "The teacher didn't," Shankar said. Naveen marched to the PE teacher anyway, his voice shaking. "I'm not saying it for me. It's not fair to everyone else."

qa.q: Where did the boy cut across?
qa.a: The muddy corner behind the tree.

qa.q: Why were Naveen's fists clenched?
qa.a: He was furious and indignant that the boy had cheated and won.

qa.q: What could Naveen do to make his case clearly?
qa.a: Stay calm, describe exactly what he saw and ask the teacher to check with other runners.

qa.q: How might Shankar see Naveen's anger?
qa.a: He understands it, but worries it won't change anything since the teacher didn't see.

grounding: Shows a child's heated reaction to seeing a rival cheat in a race.

passage: At the society's Independence Day quiz, Sachin, twelve, noticed that the team from B-block kept looking at a man in the front row, who mouthed the answers. Sachin's ears went red. When B-block won, he stood up. "That's not fair! They were told the answers!" His sister Urmila tugged his sleeve. "Sit down, people are staring." "I don't care," he said. The organiser came over, listened, and agreed to hold a tie-break round with no one in the front row.

qa.q: What did the man in the front row do?

qa.q: What made Sachin's ears go red?
qa.a: He felt angry and indignant about the cheating.

qa.q: What worked in Sachin's protest, and what could be better?
qa.a: Speaking up got a fair tie-break; he could have gone straight to the organiser rather than shouting.

qa.q: What is it like for Urmila when people stare?
qa.a: She probably feels embarrassed and anxious about the attention.

grounding: Shows a child's heated reaction to cheating at a community quiz.

passage:
"She stepped over the line! Did you see? She stepped over!"
"Jasleen, calm down."
"No, Hafsa! Neha stepped over and still tagged me. It's cheating!"
"The umpire didn't see."

"Okay. But not shouting. Let's tell Neha after the round."

passage: I'm Sangeeta. In Class 5, there was one water tap for the whole floor, and we all lined up at break. Ujjwal always pushed to the front. One hot day, I'd waited ten minutes, and he walked right past everyone and filled his bottle. I got so angry my hands shook. I shouted, "That's cheating! Back of the line!" Everyone turned. Ujjwal went red and stepped back. Later I felt a bit shaky about shouting, but I still think it was unfair. Now I'd probably say it more calmly, but I'd still say it.

qa.q: How long had Sangeeta waited at the tap?
qa.a: Ten minutes.

qa.q: How did Sangeeta feel when Ujjwal walked past everyone?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt indignant and furious, so angry that Sangeeta's hands shook.

qa.a: Say it more calmly, but still speak up against the unfairness.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal have felt when everyone turned to look?
qa.a: Ujjwal likely felt embarrassed and ashamed, going red and stepping back.

passage: Coach's note, under-12 kabaddi, Thursday. Yamini Rao. In the practice match, Sonali shouted at the other team's raider that he had crossed the bonus line without touching, and that the point shouldn't count. She was loud and pointed at him, and her voice cracked. I stopped the game. She was right about the line, and I said so. But I also told her that shouting at a player won't change a call; she can raise her hand and tell me. She nodded, still breathing hard. After the match she came to me and asked to learn the full rules. I've given her the rule sheet to read.

qa.q: What did Sonali say the raider had done?
qa.a: Crossed the bonus line without touching.

qa.q: What does Sonali's voice cracking suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt strongly indignant, upset by what she saw as unfair.

qa.a: She gave Sonali the full rule sheet to read after Sonali asked to learn the rules.

qa.q: How might the raider have felt when Sonali shouted at him?

grounding: A coach's note on a girl who reacts hotly to a rule being broken in kabaddi, and how the coach responds.

passage:
During Losar in the village near Dharamshala, the children played kabaddi in the monastery ground. Zeenat, eleven, was on the other team.

Tenzin crossed the line, got tagged, and then said, "I wasn't touched!"

Zeenat's face went red. "You were! Everyone saw!"

"No, I wasn't."

"That's cheating!" She stamped her foot. The game stopped.

An older monk walked over. "What happened?" Several children pointed at Tenzin. Tenzin looked down and walked off the field.

Zeenat was still breathing hard, but she said, "Okay, let's play again."

qa.q: Where did the children play kabaddi?
qa.a: They played kabaddi in the monastery ground.

qa.q: How did Zeenat feel when Tenzin said he wasn't touched?
qa.a: Zeenat felt indignant and angry, her face going red at the unfairness.

qa.q: How did the situation get resolved?
qa.a: An older monk asked what happened, others confirmed it, and Tenzin walked off, so the game could continue fairly.

qa.q: How might Tenzin feel walking off the field?
qa.a: Tenzin might feel embarrassed and ashamed.

grounding: During Losar, a girl reacts with emotional heat when a player cheats in kabaddi.

passage:
In Istanbul during Ramadan, the queue at the bakery for fresh pide was long before iftar. Sami, ten, and his sister Elif had waited twenty minutes.

A man walked straight to the front and asked for three loaves.

Sami's fists clenched. "Hey! There's a line!"

Elif pulled his arm. "Sami, shh."

"But it's not fair! We waited!"

The baker looked at the man. "Please join the line, sir." The man frowned and went to the back.

Sami let out a breath. Elif whispered, "You were right. But you were loud."

qa.q: How long had Sami and Elif waited?
qa.a: They had waited twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Sami feel when the man cut in line?
qa.a: Sami felt angry and indignant at the unfairness, clenching his fists.

qa.q: How could Sami express his anger more calmly next time?
qa.a: He could speak firmly but quietly, or ask the baker for help, instead of shouting.

qa.q: How might Elif have felt when Sami shouted?
qa.a: Elif felt embarrassed by the loudness, though she agreed he was right.

grounding: During Ramadan, a boy reacts with emotional heat when a man cuts in a bakery queue.

passage: It was the last day of summer sports camp at the community centre, and the relay final was close. Ira ran the third leg for her team and saw it: Tanvir, on the other team, started his run a full metre before the baton reached him. His team won by a step. Ira's face went hot. She marched to Coach Deshmukh, fists clenched. "That's cheating! He left early. Everyone saw!" Her voice cracked. Tanvir shouted, "I did not!" Coach Deshmukh raised a hand. "Let's check the video from the parents' stand." Ira stood breathing hard, arms folded, still shaking.

qa.q: Which leg did Ira run?
qa.a: She ran the third leg for her team.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling when she marched to Coach Deshmukh?
qa.a: She felt angry and indignant at what looked like cheating, so strongly that her voice cracked.

qa.q: How could Ira raise the complaint so it gets heard?
